nameStory: The Thick-billed Murre gets its name from its notably robust, chunky bill that's thicker than its close cousin, the Common Murre. The word 'murre' itself comes from an old Scottish term describing the bird's distinctive purring call that echoes off coastal cliffs. It's also called Brünnich's guillemot, honoring Danish zoologist Morten Thrane Brünnich who first described the species.
description: The Thick-billed Murre is a stocky seabird that looks like a cross between a penguin and a duck, dressed in a formal black-and-white tuxedo. These chunky birds are excellent underwater swimmers, using their wings like flippers to chase fish beneath the waves. They're medium-sized seabirds, roughly the size of a small duck, with a distinctive upright posture when standing on rocky ledges. In winter, you'll spot them bobbing on ocean waters off New England's coast, often in large flocks.

idTips.label: Thick, pointed bill
idTips.description: The bill is noticeably chunky and triangular, feeling solid and heavy-looking, with a thin white line along the edge during breeding season

idTips.label: Black and white plumage
idTips.description: Deep chocolate-black head, back, and wings contrast sharply with bright white underparts that look crisp as fresh snow

idTips.label: Stocky body shape
idTips.description: Compact, barrel-shaped body with short neck gives them a chunky, robust appearance like a feathered football

idTips.label: Upright standing posture
idTips.description: When on land, stands tall and straight like a tiny penguin, often swaying slightly as they balance on webbed feet

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Dives completely underwater and 'flies' beneath the surface, often popping up unexpectedly several yards away

habitat: In New England, you'll find Thick-billed Murres exclusively in offshore ocean waters, particularly over deeper waters beyond the continental shelf. They prefer cold, nutrient-rich waters where small fish are abundant, often appearing during winter storms when they're blown closer to shore. Look for them from coastal headlands, whale-watching boats, or sometimes from beaches after major weather events.

seasonality.spring: Murres begin moving north to Arctic breeding grounds, becoming less common in New England waters. Look for birds transitioning to breeding plumage with cleaner black-and-white patterns.
seasonality.summer: Rarely seen in New England during summer as they're busy nesting on remote Arctic cliffs. Any summer sightings are usually non-breeding individuals.
seasonality.fall: Return migration brings them back to New England waters in increasing numbers. Watch for mixed flocks of adults and juveniles with slightly duller plumage.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for sightings as birds winter in offshore waters. Often seen in large flocks, especially during and after coastal storms that bring them closer to shore.

funFact: Thick-billed Murres can dive to depths of over 650 feet underwater – deeper than a 60-story building is tall – and hold their breath for up to 4 minutes while chasing fish in the pitch-black depths, using their wings to literally fly through the water.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Common Murre, but the Thick-billed Murre's bill is noticeably chunkier and more triangular, while Common Murre has a longer, thinner, more pointed bill. Remember: 'Thick bill, thick bird' – Thick-billed Murres also tend to look stockier overall.
contextualKnowledge: The alternate name 'guillemot' can be confusing since there are also birds called Black Guillemot in New England, but they're much smaller with different markings. In North America, 'murre' is the preferred common name, while 'guillemot' is more commonly used in Europe for the same species.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Common Murre, the Thick-billed Murre has a noticeably more robust, triangular bill versus the Common Murre's longer, thinner bill. Thick-billed Murres also tend to have a slightly more compact, stockier body shape. During breeding season, Thick-billed Murres show a distinctive thin white line along the bill edge that Common Murres lack.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Murres are much more likely to be seen in New England than their close relative, the Thick-billed Murre.
